跟着新员工王さん走过入职头两年：自我介绍、报连相、接电话、见客户、开会、道歉、聚: Follow new employee Wang through his first two years at the company: self-introductions, 「報連相」 (reporting, informing, and consulting), answering the phone, meeting clients, meetings, apologies, after-work drinks, performance reviews, and farewells.
入职第一天的自我介绍: Introducing yourself on your first day at work
四月一日早上九点，青叶商事营业部的早会。课长森田把刚入职的王さん带到大家面前，请: It's 9:00 a.m. on April 1, at the morning meeting of the sales department at Aoba Shoji. Section Manager Morita brings Wang, who has just joined the company, in front of everyone and asks him to give a short self-introduction. A dozen or so coworkers are standing there watching him, and Wang's palms are drenched in sweat.
营业部课长，五十岁出头，要求严格、话不多，但很留意下属: Section manager in the sales department, in his early fifties; strict and a man of few words, but keeps a close eye on his staff
中国上海人，在日本读完大学，今天第一天上班: From Shanghai, China; finished university in Japan, and today is his first day at work
入职第五年的前辈，亲切爱笑，负责带王さん: A senpai in her fifth year at the company; friendly and quick to smile, and in charge of showing Wang the ropes
王さん是全场最「下」的人，对课长和所有同事都要用丁宁语加自谦语。课长对部下用普通: Wang is the "lowest" person in the room, so with the section manager and every coworker he needs to use the polite (です/ます) style plus humble language (kenjōgo). The section manager uses the plain style with his subordinates; that's the normal way for a superior to talk to someone below them, not rudeness. His senpai Sato speaks to the new hire fairly casually, but Wang should still use 「です・ます」 with her.
大家早上好。这位是今天起加入营业部的王さん。王さん，说两句吧。: Good morning, everyone. This is Wang, who's joining the sales department as of today. Wang, a few words, please.
被点名时先干脆地答一声「はい！」再往前走一步。日本职场很看重这一声：声音清楚、马: When your name is called, first give a crisp 「はい！」, then take a step forward. Japanese workplaces put a lot of weight on this one word: answering clearly and right away says "I'm paying attention." If you hesitate and stay silent, people will assume you aren't prepared.
大家早上好。从今天起在营业部承蒙大家照顾，我叫王浩。: Good morning, everyone. My name is Wang Hao, and starting today I'll be in your care here in the sales department.
「お世話になります」是「今后要麻烦大家了」，第一天进新地方的固定开场。用「本日」: 「お世話になります」 means "I'll be relying on all of you from now on," and it's the standard opener on your first day somewhere new. 「本日」 is more formal than 「今日」, and 「と申します」 puts yourself in a humble position. Put the three together, and your very first sentence already sounds like a working professional.
我来自中国上海。来日本今年是第四年。: I'm from Shanghai, China. This is my fourth year in Japan.
爱好是做饭，周末常包饺子。: My hobby is cooking, and on weekends I often make gyoza.
我是第一次工作，应该会有很多不懂的地方。: This is my first time in the working world, so I'm sure there will be a lot of things I don't know.
我做错的时候，请大家不客气地指出来。: When I make mistakes, please don't hesitate to point them out.
这句是在主动「请别人批评我」。日本前辈其实很犹豫要不要指出新人的错，怕伤人。你先: With this sentence, you're actively "asking people to criticize you." Japanese senpai are actually quite hesitant to point out a new employee's mistakes, for fear of hurting their feelings. Saying this first is like handing everyone a permission slip, and only then will people feel free to teach you honestly.
我会努力，争取早一天能帮上大家的忙。: I'll work hard so that I can be of use to all of you as soon as possible.
请大家多多关照。: I look forward to working with you all.
说完这句要停一下再鞠躬（先说后鞠躬，叫「語先後礼」），弯腰三十度左右，数两拍再起: After saying this, pause for a moment and then bow (speaking first and bowing afterward is called 「語先後礼」). Bend about 30 degrees, hold for two beats, then straighten up. If you lower your head while still talking, your voice gets muffled toward the floor and people can't hear you clearly.
王さん，我是坐你旁边的佐藤。请多关照呀。: Wang, I'm Sato, at the desk next to yours. Looking forward to working with you!
王さん，谢谢。一开始出错很正常，出错了马上说就行。: Thanks, Wang. It's natural to make mistakes at first, so if you make one, just tell us right away.
「自己紹介をする」。早会、聚餐、新项目开始时都会被要求做，最好准备好三十秒版本: 「自己紹介をする」. You'll be asked to give one at morning meetings, after-work dinners, and the start of new projects, so it's best to have a 30-second version ready
职场、电话、邮件里代替「今日」。「本日はよろしくお願いいたします」: Used in place of 「今日」 at work, on the phone, and in emails. 「本日はよろしくお願いいたします」
承蒙关照: thank you for your support (lit. "I'll be in your care")
第一次去新地方时说；已经受到照顾后改用「お世話になっております」: Said when you first go somewhere new; once you've already been receiving someone's help, switch to 「お世話になっております」
只用在自己或自己公司的人身上：「王と申します」: Used only for yourself or people from your own company: 「王と申します」
「営業」是跑客户、卖东西的工作；「営業に出る」= 出去跑客户: 「営業」 is the work of calling on clients and selling things; 「営業に出る」 = to go out on sales calls
社会人、上班族: working adult, member of the workforce
学生毕业开始工作就叫社会人。「社会人一年目」= 工作第一年: Once students graduate and start working, they're called 「社会人」. 「社会人一年目」 = first year in the workforce
「一言お願いします」= 请简单说几句。被这样点名时别讲太长，三十秒到一分钟: 「一言お願いします」 = please say a few words. When you're called on like this, don't go on too long: 30 seconds to a minute
别客气、尽管: without holding back, feel free to
「遠慮なくご指摘ください」「遠慮なく聞いてね」，邀请对方放开说: 「遠慮なくご指摘ください」, 「遠慮なく聞いてね」: inviting the other person to speak freely
「ミスを指摘される」= 被指出错误；对上用「ご指摘」: 「ミスを指摘される」 = to have a mistake pointed out; toward superiors, use 「ご指摘」
有用、帮得上忙: to be useful, to be of help
「お役に立てるように」= 为了能帮上忙；说自己时常加「お」表示谦和: 「お役に立てるように」 = so that I can be of help; when talking about yourself, 「お」 is often added to sound modest
努力、加油: to try hard, to do one's best
自我介绍结尾说「頑張ります」，比「頑張りたいです」更有决心: Ending a self-introduction with 「頑張ります」 shows more determination than 「頑張りたいです」
「隣の席」= 旁边的座位。新人常和带自己的前辈坐在一起: 「隣の席」 = the seat next to you. New employees often sit with the senpai who's showing them the ropes
进入新环境时用「なります」；关系已经开始后用「なっております」: Use 「なります」 when you're entering a new environment; use 「なっております」 once the relationship has already begun
这不是在感谢某件具体的事，而是确认「我们之间有关系了」。第一天说「お世話になりま: This isn't thanks for any specific thing; it's a way of confirming that "we now have a relationship." Saying 「お世話になります」 on your first day means you'll be relying on everyone from now on; after that, opening every phone call and email with 「お世話になっております」 keeps workplace relationships running smoothly. Leave it out, and Japanese people will feel your opening is too abrupt.
从今天起承蒙关照，我姓王。: My name is Wang, and starting today I'll be in your care.
一直以来承蒙关照。: Thank you, as always, for your support.
为了能……而努力: do one's best so that one can ...
动词可能形 + ように頑張ります: Verb potential form + ように頑張ります
比只说「頑張ります」多了一个具体的目标，听的人知道你想变成什么样。「役に立てるよ: Compared with just saying 「頑張ります」, this adds a concrete goal, so the listener knows what you want to become. 「役に立てるように」 and 「早く慣れるように」 are the ones new employees use most. Note that the verb in front should be in the potential form, or be a verb like 「慣れる」 or 「なる」 that you can't directly control.
我会努力尽快熟悉工作。: I'll do my best to get used to the job quickly.
我会努力争取能一个人负责客户。: I'll do my best so that I can handle clients on my own.
请不要客气地……: please feel free to ..., please don't hesitate to ...
遠慮なく + 动词て形 + ください（更礼貌：ご〜ください）: 遠慮なく + verb て-form + ください (more polite: ご〜ください)
日本人怕给别人添麻烦，所以常常「想说也不说」。这个句型是在主动打开对方的嘴。新人: Japanese people are afraid of causing others trouble, so they often "don't say it even when they want to." This pattern actively invites the other person to open up. When a new employee says 「遠慮なくご指摘ください」 to a senpai, or a senpai says 「遠慮なく聞いてね」 to a new employee, each is making it easy for the other to speak up.
有不懂的地方请尽管问。: If there's anything you don't understand, please don't hesitate to ask.
如果您注意到什么，请尽管说。: If you notice anything, please don't hesitate to tell me.
入职第一天的早会、调到新部门、第一次参加项目会议时，先说「お世話になります」，再: At the morning meeting on your first day, when you transfer to a new department, or at your first project meeting, start with 「お世話になります」, then give your name, your background, a line or two of personal information, and your resolve. Thirty seconds to a minute is ideal.
中国人容易讲太长，把学历、获奖都说一遍，日本人会觉得在炫耀。也别反复说「日本語が: Many learners tend to go on too long, listing their education and every award they've won, and Japanese listeners will think they're showing off. Also, don't keep apologizing with 「日本語が下手ですが」; saying 「まだまだですが」 once is enough, and then move right on to "I'll do my best."
大家其实不太在意你讲得多流利，而是在看你的态度：声音清不清楚、有没有笑、愿不愿意: People don't really care how fluent you are; they're watching your attitude: whether your voice is clear, whether you smile, and whether you're willing to be taught. When senpai hear 「遠慮なくご指摘ください」, they think "this one will be easy to mentor," and that's how trust starts with a first impression.
第一天王さん紧张得声音发抖，说完才发现早会只给了他一分钟。散会后，平时一句闲话都: On his first day, Wang was so nervous that his voice shook, and only after he finished did he realize the morning meeting had given him just one minute. After the meeting broke up, Section Manager Morita, who never makes small talk, came over and said just one thing: 「間違えたら、すぐ言えばいい」. Many people meeting a Japanese boss for the first time find them cold and quiet, and can't tell what mood they're in. But strict people are often the ones who watch most closely: he'll remember which day you were the first to arrive, and who poured you a cup of tea. What a new employee can do on day one is actually simple: arrive five minutes early, remember the names of the few people sitting around you, and answer 「はい」 right away when you're called. These little things aren't mere formalities; they tell everyone "I'm going to take you seriously." And don't worry that your Japanese isn't perfect: actively saying "please point out my mistakes" earns more trust than pretending to understand everything.
第一天在早会上做自我介绍，最合适的开头是？: You're introducing yourself at the morning meeting on your first day. What's the most appropriate way to begin?
第一天用「お世話になります」（今后要麻烦大家），名字用「と申します」。「いつもお: On your first day, use 「お世話になります」 (I'll be relying on you all from now on) and give your name with 「と申します」. 「いつもお世話になっております」 is for after a relationship has already begun, and 「申し上げます」 sounds unnatural with your name.
课长说「王さん、一言お願いします」，你应该怎么做？: The section manager says 「王さん、一言お願いします」. What should you do?
马上答「はい！」，讲三十秒到一分钟: Answer 「はい！」 right away and speak for 30 seconds to a minute
先谦虚地推辞「いえいえ、私なんか」: First decline modestly with 「いえいえ、私なんか」
详细讲十分钟自己的经历: Talk about your background in detail for ten minutes
笑着点头，不出声: Smile and nod without saying anything
「一言」就是简短几句。马上回应「はい」是职场基本功，推辞会耽误大家的早会时间。: 「一言」 means just a few brief words. Responding with 「はい」 right away is a basic workplace skill, and declining would eat into everyone's morning meeting time.
想请前辈们以后发现你的错误时直接告诉你，最合适的是？: You want your senpai to tell you directly whenever they notice a mistake from now on. What's the most appropriate thing to say?
「遠慮なくご指摘ください」是主动请对方指出问题，态度谦虚又积极。「教えてもいいで: 「遠慮なくご指摘ください」 actively asks the other person to point out problems, and it's both humble and proactive. 「教えてもいいですよ」 sounds like a superior talking down to a subordinate and is extremely rude.
